sources.headline: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
sources.text: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

Ukrainian drone attack on Saint Petersburg kills one, sets refinery ablaze
EUROPE

A large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's second-largest city Saint Petersburg killed at least one person and hospitalised another five on Sunday. The attack – which also sparked fires at an oil refinery and depot – comes as Kyiv accused Russia of violating Washington's "energy ceasefire" dozens of times.   

Issued on: 18/10/2026 - 14:03
Modified: 18/10/2026 - 15:07

4 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
An oil terminal ablaze in Saint Petersburg following Ukrainian drone attacks on October 18 2026, in Russia. © AFP

Ukraine hit Saint Petersburg with a large-scale drone attack, causing fires at an oil refinery and depot, Moscow said Sunday, as Kyiv accused Russia of violating US President Donald Trump's "energy ceasefire" dozens of times and leaving tens of thousands without power.

Trump last week announced an "energy ceasefire"– which neither side said they agreed to beforehand – that quickly collapsed, with Moscow continuing strikes on Ukraine's power grid and Kyiv eventually resuming hits on Russian oil refineries.

READ MORE

Trump has been angered by Kyiv's strikes on Russian refineries – which he says are contributing to a surge in global fuel prices.

On Sunday, Ukraine hit Russia's second city as its ties with Washington strained in recent days.

Kyiv says its retaliatory strikes are fair retribution for years of Russia's offensive and destruction of its energy infrastructure.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia Sunday of hitting Kyiv's energy, oil and gas facilities 76 times since Trump announced his ceasefire.

Saint Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city – President Vladimir Putin's hometown – in the night-time strikes.

Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.

Flights were restricted at the city's Pulkovo airport, Beglov said, adding that 12 housing blocks were also damaged.

Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit in the city and Ozon – Russia's second largest retailer – also reported a hit on its logistics centre.

The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.

Ukraine has attacked Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin's dragging offensive but large-scale hits on Russia's main cities are rare.

US-led peace talks have not led to a breakthrough. In a fifth year of war, few see a way out.

"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking – it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.

Sergei, another resident of the city who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.

"I don't know if I was scared; what must be will be," he told AFP.

"My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I'd better fill up."

Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.

'Getting on my nerves'
Ukraine has hit Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin's offensive, but large-scale attacks on the cities are rare. © AFP

Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.

He said a woman and three children were hospitalised "with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning" in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.

Smoke rose above Saint Petersburg's shipyards and was visible from the historic city centre, on the banks of the Neva River.

"I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire," 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.

"They're getting on my nerves already," he added, referring to Ukraine.

Putin this week appeared in military uniform and said Moscow intended to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine by force.

'Their bet on war is paying off'

The attack came a day after Zelensky called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow to end the war and as he denounced Trump's move to block new sanctions on Russia.

On Sunday, he said Russian strikes hit substations in four Ukrainian regions, leaving "tens of thousands of families without power".

He has warned Moscow is trying to leave Ukrainians without heat and power ahead of winter.

Russian strikes also killed two people in an "agricultural enterprise" in the western Volyn region – bordering NATO member Poland – on Sunday, the wartime leader said.

"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements," Zelensky said, adding:

"On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting."

Trump this week blocked a package of new sanctions on Russia which was meant to target Putin, as well as Russia's energy and defence sectors.

The US leader also signed an agreement with Moscow this month to buy diesel, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of elections.

Kyiv and its European allies worry the White House is taking Russia's side in Europe's worst conflict since WWII.

"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance," Zelensky said Sunday.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

sources.headline: Russia: Huge flames and smoke rise over St Petersburg after drone strikes
sources.text:
Footage shared on social media showed a major blaze at a warehouse operated by Ozon, Russia's second-largest online retailer, which said its logistics centre had been struck. Other images showed thick smoke rising from the area of the St Petersburg Oil Terminal, while an oil refinery and depot were also reportedly hit.
St Petersburg's governor, Alexander Beglov, confirmed that air-defence systems had been activated after a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city overnight, while Leningrad Region governor Alexander Drozdenko initially reported that 126 drones had been shot down over the surrounding region. He later raised that figure to 144, with some reports putting it at 145.
The assault set the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot alight and struck infrastructure in several districts of the city. Beglov said one person was killed and five others were injured, while operations at Pulkovo Airport were temporarily restricted for safety reasons.
The strikes came as President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after briefly suspending them following Donald Trump’s declaration of an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. Neither side formally confirmed the arrangement, and Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out 76 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure over the following week, including strikes on substations in four regions that left tens of thousands of families without power.
The latest exchange underlines the continuing struggle over energy infrastructure, with both sides treating refineries, terminals and power grids as central targets in a war that shows no sign of abating.

sources.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the US formally siding with Russia would be a "historic mistake" - as Ukrainian drones attacked oil facilities in St Petersburg.

sources.text: President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed overt frustration with the United States in an interview with The Financial Times. He had paused the strikes to comply with a demand from the United States.

sources.headline: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
sources.text:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham says goodbye to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after their meeting at 10 Downing Street in London, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026.
Alberto Pezzali/AP
hide caption
Alberto Pezzali/AP
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze. A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery. Zelenskyy complains about U.S. behavior in recent days The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire. Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying. Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin. Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress. Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump." He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us." Starlink speed limits affect Ukraine's ability to defend itself In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle." Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history." The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said. Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump. The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted." Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said. "It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations. Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.
